lessons.title: Lay out a complete page with semantic landmark elements
lessons.summary: Replace anonymous divs with header, nav, main, section, article, aside and footer, and learn exactly what each region means.
lessons.goal: Assemble a full page skeleton from the seven structural elements, with each one in its correct place.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every professional page you will ever build starts from the same structural frame: a header, navigation, one main content area, and a footer. Getting these elements right is not decoration — screen readers use them as jump targets, search engines use them to find your primary content, and teammates use them to understand your layout at a glance. Once this skeleton is second nature, every layout you write becomes faster and cleaner.

Read the section on main and memorise its one-per-page rule.
Study the article vs section decision rule — it is the part people get wrong most.

sections.heading: Named regions instead of anonymous boxes
sections.body:
A div is a box with no meaning: it groups content and nothing more. HTML5 added a set of structural elements that behave exactly like divs visually but declare what their content is for. Browsers, screen readers, search engines and reader modes all understand these names.

The seven you will use constantly are header, nav, main, section, article, aside and footer. Learning them is not about memorising tags — it is about learning the one question each element answers: who is this content for, and what role does it play on the page?

None of these elements changes how the page looks. They are pure structure. That is the point: meaning and appearance are separate jobs, and CSS handles the second one.

sections.heading: header, nav and footer
sections.body:
header marks introductory content for its nearest ancestor: a logo, a title, a tagline, often the site navigation. It is not only for the top of the page — an article can open with its own header holding the title and publish date.

nav wraps a block of major navigation links: the site menu, a table of contents, breadcrumbs. Not every group of links qualifies. A paragraph with two inline links, or a short list of legal links in the footer, works fine without nav — flooding a page with nav elements makes the real navigation harder to find for screen-reader users who jump between them.

footer is the mirror of header: closing content for its nearest ancestor. On the page level that means copyright lines, contact details and secondary links. Like header, it can also appear inside an article to hold metadata such as the author or tags.

sections.heading: main: exactly one per page
sections.body:
main wraps the content that is unique to the current page — the reason this URL exists. Everything repeated across pages stays outside it: the site header, the site navigation, the footer.

The rule that matters: one main per page, and it cannot be nested inside article, aside, header, footer or nav. Assistive technologies rely on this. The single main is the landmark a screen-reader user jumps to in order to skip past the banner and menus, so a page with two mains — or with the menu accidentally inside main — defeats the entire feature.

If you find yourself wanting a second main, you actually want section or article. If you find your nav inside main, your nav is in the wrong place (unless it is genuinely page-specific navigation, like a table of contents for the article — that one may live inside main).
sections.code:
<body>
  <header>...site banner...</header>
  <main>
    <!-- only this page's unique content -->
  </main>
  <footer>...site footer...</footer>
</body>

sections.heading: article vs section: the decision rule
sections.body:
These two cause the most hesitation, but one question settles almost every case: would this block still make sense if you lifted it out and published it somewhere else on its own?

If yes, it is an article. A blog post, a news story, a forum comment, a product card, a widget in a dashboard — each is a self-contained composition. The name misleads people: article is not only for written articles, it is for anything independently distributable. An RSS feed is a good mental test — if the block could be an entry in a feed, it is an article.

If no — the block only makes sense as a chapter of the surrounding page — it is a section. A landing page's 'Pricing' and 'Testimonials' blocks are sections: meaningful here, meaningless alone. A section should almost always start with a heading; if you cannot think of a natural heading for it, you probably wanted a plain div.

They nest both ways. A long article can be divided into sections (chapters of the post). A section can contain articles (a 'Latest news' section holding three post teasers).

sections.heading: aside: related, not required
sections.body:
aside holds content that is tangentially related to what surrounds it — the reader could skip it without losing the thread. Classic examples: a pull quote, a glossary box, a list of related posts, an author bio, advertising.

The common misunderstanding is to equate aside with 'sidebar column'. Position is irrelevant. An aside can render inline, below, or floated right; what makes it an aside is the relationship of its content to the main flow. Conversely, a sidebar column that contains your primary navigation is a nav, not an aside.

An aside placed inside an article is understood as related to that article (a note about the trail in this post). An aside placed directly in body or main is understood as related to the page as a whole (a site-wide newsletter box).

sections.heading: Nesting: landmarks inside landmarks
sections.body:
The structural elements are designed to compose. header and footer attach to their nearest sectioning ancestor, so a page header and an article header coexist without conflict — one introduces the site, the other introduces the post.

Common, correct combinations: nav inside the page header; header and footer inside an article; sections inside an article to split it into chapters; an aside inside main next to the article it relates to; articles inside a section that groups them.

Combinations to avoid: main inside anything other than body (or a plain wrapper div); a footer inside a footer or header inside a header; nav wrapped around every link cluster. When unsure, keep the skeleton shallow — depth should follow the content's real structure, not habit.

sections.heading: The complete page skeleton
sections.body:
Put together, nearly every content page follows one shape: header with nav at the top, one main holding the unique content (articles and sections, with asides where relevant), and a footer at the bottom.

Memorise this frame. When you start a new page, type it before anything else, then fill it in. It keeps you from ever reaching for a div where a landmark belongs, and it means every page you produce is navigable by assistive technology from the first minute.

lessons.title: See exactly what semantic markup buys you over div soup
lessons.summary: Compare a div-only page with its semantic twin and understand the concrete wins: search ranking, screen-reader landmarks, maintainability and reader modes.
lessons.goal: Convert a div-soup page to semantic markup and articulate why each conversion pays off — and where a div is still the right tool.
lessons.whyItMatters: Semantic markup is one of the cheapest quality wins in web development: it costs nothing at render time and pays out in search visibility, accessibility compliance, and code your colleagues can read without a map. Companies get sued over inaccessible pages and lose traffic over unparseable ones — both problems often start with a wall of anonymous divs. Knowing when a div is still correct is part of the same skill.

Work through the sections on SEO, landmarks and maintainability to see who benefits and how.
Read 'When div is still the right choice' — semantics is not about banning div.

Complete tasks 1–5, converting the structural divs but deliberately keeping the styling div.

coding.intro: You will refactor a div-soup news page into semantic markup, keeping one deliberate div to prove you know when div is still correct.

sections.heading: The same page, twice
sections.body:
Take a small news page: site title, menu, one story, copyright line. You can build it entirely from divs with descriptive class names, and it will render perfectly. Developers call this pattern div soup — a page whose structure exists only in class names that no machine understands.

Now build the identical page with header, nav, main, article and footer. The rendering is pixel-for-pixel the same, because these elements carry no default styling beyond display: block.

So why bother? Because HTML is not only read by browsers painting pixels. It is read by search crawlers, screen readers, reader modes, translation tools, scrapers, and by the next developer. Every one of those readers gets more from the second version. The rest of this lesson itemises exactly what they get.

sections.heading: What search engines get
sections.body:
Crawlers try to answer one question about your page: what is the actual content here, as opposed to the chrome around it? Semantic markup answers it directly. main says 'the unique content is here'; article says 'this block is a self-contained piece'; nav and footer say 'this is boilerplate, weight it lightly'.

With div soup, the crawler falls back to heuristics — text density, link ratios, position — which work most of the time and fail quietly the rest. Failure looks like your navigation labels appearing in a search snippet, or a sidebar promo being indexed as the page topic.

Semantics is not a magic ranking boost, and no honest source claims it is. What it gives you is accurate extraction: the engine indexes what you meant. Structured content also feeds features such as snippets and article previews more reliably.

sections.heading: What screen readers get: landmarks
sections.body:
Screen readers map the structural elements to landmarks — named regions a user can list and jump between with a keystroke. header becomes banner, nav becomes navigation, main becomes main, aside becomes complementary, footer becomes contentinfo.

This changes how a page is used. Instead of listening through the site header and full menu on every page load, a screen-reader user jumps straight to main. Instead of hunting for the menu, they jump to navigation. Surveys of screen-reader users consistently show landmark and heading navigation among the primary ways they move through pages.

Div soup produces zero landmarks. The page becomes a single flat stream, and every visit means wading from the top. You could bolt landmarks onto divs with ARIA role attributes, but the first rule of ARIA is to prefer the native element that already carries the role — <header> over <div role="banner"> — because it is shorter, harder to get wrong, and impossible to forget.
sections.code:
<!-- Landmarks a screen reader announces: -->
<header>   <!-- banner -->
<nav>      <!-- navigation -->
<main>     <!-- main -->
<aside>    <!-- complementary -->
<footer>   <!-- contentinfo -->

sections.heading: What your team gets: code that explains itself
sections.body:
Open an unfamiliar file and find <footer> on line 80 — you instantly know what that block is and roughly what belongs in it. Find <div class="bx-3"> and you know nothing until you trace the CSS.

Semantic elements act as enforced, standardised comments. Unlike class names, they cannot drift into private jargon, they survive CSS rewrites and framework migrations, and they are identical across every codebase in the industry. A new hire who knows HTML already knows your page structure.

They also give you resilient styling hooks. A rule like main > article works regardless of what the design system renames its classes this quarter. Teams that lean on structure for layout selectors ship fewer of the 'renamed a class, broke a page' regressions.

sections.heading: What reader modes and other tools get
sections.body:
Browsers ship reader modes that strip a page down to its content for comfortable reading. Their extraction logic leans heavily on structure: an article inside main is a strong signal of 'the content'; nav, aside and footer are strong signals of 'discard this'.

On a semantic page, reader mode produces a clean, complete story. On div soup it guesses — sometimes dropping half the article, sometimes including the cookie banner. The same extraction problem is faced by read-later apps, text-to-speech services, translation pipelines, AI assistants summarising the page, and print stylesheets. One markup decision feeds all of them.

This is the general principle worth internalising: you do not control which software will consume your HTML over its lifetime. Writing semantically is how you stay correct for consumers that do not exist yet.

sections.heading: When div is still the right choice
sections.body:
Semantics does not mean 'never write div'. A div is correct precisely when a block has no meaning to convey — it exists so CSS can grab it. Wrappers that centre a layout, flex and grid containers, styled cards, overlay backdrops: these are presentational grouping, and div is the honest element for them.

The test is simple: if you removed all styling, would this grouping still communicate something about the content? If yes, pick the semantic element. If the grouping only exists for the stylesheet, keep the div. Forcing section onto every styling wrapper is as wrong as div soup — it buries the real landmarks in noise.

The same logic applies inline: span is the phrasing-level div, correct when you need a styling or scripting hook on a run of text that has no semantic identity of its own.

sections.heading: Headings inside sectioned content
sections.body:
HTML5 originally proposed an 'outline algorithm' in which every section or article could restart at h1 and nesting depth would determine the real level. No browser or screen reader ever implemented it, and the idea has been removed from the standard. Do not structure headings as if it existed.

The working rule: the page has one heading outline, numbered explicitly by you. One h1 for the page; an article or section directly under it starts at h2; a subsection inside that uses h3; and no level is skipped going down. Sectioning elements group content, but they do not renumber anything.

In practice, put a heading at the top of every section and article — it names the region for sighted scanners and screen-reader users alike — and choose its level from the document outline, not from the element it happens to sit in.

lessons.title: Build a correct data table with rows, cells and scoped headers
lessons.summary: Learn table, tr, td and th — including the scope attribute from day one — and when a table is the right tool at all.
lessons.goal: Construct a small data table with properly scoped header cells and understand the row-based model behind every HTML table.
lessons.whyItMatters: Real applications are full of genuinely tabular data: invoices, schedules, comparison charts, admin dashboards. A table built correctly — headers marked as headers, with scope declared — is readable to everyone including screen-reader users, who hear each cell announced with its column and row context. A table built from divs or with plain bold cells forces users to count columns in their head, and it happens constantly in production code.
steps: Read the theory on what a table is and the rows-first mental model.
Study th and the scope attribute — do not skip scope; it is part of correct table syntax here from the start.
Read when a table is the right choice and when it is layout abuse.
Open the starter code: an empty table shell for planet data.
Add the header row with three scoped th cells (tasks 1–2).
Add the three data rows (tasks 3–4) and run the checks.
lessons.explanation: The table is written row by row: each tr is one horizontal slice, and the cells inside it fall into columns purely by position. The first row uses th instead of td because its cells label the columns rather than hold data, and scope="col" states that explicitly — each th governs the cells below it. With that in place, a screen reader can announce 'Moons: 2' when a user lands on the second cell of the Mars row, instead of just the bare number.
lessons.example:
Imagine reading '25 hours' aloud to someone with no table visible. Useless — until you add its context: 'Mars, day length, 25 hours'.

That context is exactly what th and scope encode. A sighted reader reconstructs it by glancing up the column; a screen reader can only provide it if the markup says which cells are headers and which direction they apply.

lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a compact, borderless grid: a bold header row (Planet, Moons, Day length) above three aligned data rows.
commonMistakes: Marking header cells as bold td instead of th. Bold styling is invisible to assistive technology; only th declares 'this cell labels others'.
Omitting scope because the table 'is simple'. Adding scope costs seconds and keeps the table unambiguous as it inevitably grows.
Writing cells column by column in your head. HTML tables are strictly row-major: every tr is one row, and uneven cell counts between rows shear the grid.
Using a table to position page elements. Layout is CSS's job; tables are for data with a genuine row-and-column meaning.
lessons.proTip: Before writing any table, sketch it as a spreadsheet in a comment: header line first, one line per row. If you cannot express the content as a spreadsheet, it is not tabular data and does not belong in a table.

coding.intro: You will build a three-column planets table from an empty shell, marking every header cell with th and scope from the start.

sections.heading: What a table really is
sections.body:
An HTML table is a two-dimensional grid for data whose meaning comes from its position: each cell is defined by the row and the column it sits in. Think of a spreadsheet — a price list, a league standing, a timetable. If the row and column intersection carries meaning, you have tabular data.

Four elements are enough for a basic table. table is the container for the whole grid. tr (table row) defines one horizontal slice. td (table data) is an ordinary cell inside a row. th (table header) is a cell that labels other cells rather than holding data itself.

Everything in a table must live inside cells. Text placed directly inside table or tr, outside any td or th, is invalid — browsers actually hoist such stray text out above the table, which is a classic source of mysteriously misplaced content.
sections.code: one cell another cell

sections.heading: Rows first: the mental model
sections.body:
HTML tables are written strictly row by row. There is no element for a column of cells — you never write 'the Moons column'; you write each row and the columns emerge from cell positions. The second cell of every row forms the second column, and so on.

This has a practical consequence: every row must contain the same number of cells (spanning, covered in a later lesson, is the controlled exception). If one tr has three cells and the next has two, the grid shears and the browser leaves a gap. When a table looks broken, count cells per row first — it is the cause more often than anything else.

A good habit is to draft the table as plain text before writing tags: 'Planet | Moons | Day length' on line one, then one line per planet. Each draft line becomes one tr, each pipe-separated value one cell. This makes miscounts visible before they become markup.
sections.code: Mars 2 25 hours

sections.heading: th: cells that label other cells
sections.body:
A header cell uses th instead of td. Browsers render th bold and centred by default, but as always the styling is incidental — the meaning is the point: this cell names what the cells in its row or column contain.

The most common pattern is a first row made entirely of th elements, one per column. Tables can also have row headers: a first column of th cells, where each row is labelled by its first cell (think of a nutrition table where each row starts with 'Protein', 'Fat', 'Sugar').

Both patterns can coexist in one table — column headers across the top and row headers down the left side. That is exactly when the question 'which cells does this th apply to?' stops being guessable, which is why th has a companion attribute you should use from your very first table.
sections.code:
<tr>
  <th scope="col">Planet</th>
  <th scope="col">Moons</th>
  <th scope="col">Day length</th>
</tr>

sections.heading: scope: which direction a header points
sections.body:
The scope attribute states which cells a th governs. scope="col" means 'I label the column below me'. scope="row" means 'I label the row to my right'. Two more values, rowgroup and colgroup, exist for spanned headers and are covered in the lesson on complex tables.

Screen readers use scope to give every data cell its context. When a user navigates to a cell, the reader announces the associated headers first: 'Mars, Moons, 2'. Without scope, readers fall back to guessing from table shape — which works for trivial tables and fails silently the moment a layout gets slightly unusual.

Make scope a habit, not an upgrade: every th you ever write should carry either scope="col" or scope="row". It documents your intent for machines and for the developer who extends the table next year.
sections.code:
<!-- Column headers -->
<th scope="col">Moons</th>

<!-- A row header, first cell of its row -->
<th scope="row">Mars</th>

sections.heading: When a table is right — and when it is wrong
sections.body:
Use a table when the data is genuinely two-dimensional: each row is one record, each column one property, and the intersection is a fact. Price lists, results, timetables, feature comparisons, financial statements — all tables.

Do not use a table to arrange unrelated page parts into a visual grid. In the era before CSS layout, entire sites were built as giant invisible tables; the technique survives in old code and email templates. On the modern web it is wrong twice over: screen readers announce it as data ('table with 3 rows and 2 columns...') when it is not, and CSS grid or flexbox does the layout job better.

The inverse mistake is newer: rebuilding real data grids out of styled divs because a CSS framework makes that easy. If the content is a spreadsheet at heart, divs throw away the row-and-column semantics that make it navigable. Tabular data deserves table markup.

sections.heading: What you see by default
sections.body:
An unstyled table renders more plainly than most people expect: no borders, no gridlines, minimal spacing — just aligned text, with th cells bold and centred. The classic 'lines around every cell' look is CSS, typically border on cells plus border-collapse: collapse on the table.

The old border="1" attribute on table still draws crude borders in browsers, and you will meet it in legacy code and tutorials. It is presentational leftovers from early HTML: fine for a ten-second debugging peek, not for real styling — keep appearance in CSS.

Two default behaviours worth knowing: columns size themselves to their content, so cell widths shift as data changes unless CSS fixes them; and a table only grows as wide as it needs, not to the full page width. Neither is a bug — both are just the unstyled starting point you will later shape with CSS.

lessons.title: Structure tables with caption, head, body, foot and column groups
lessons.summary: Add caption, thead, tbody, tfoot and colgroup/col to a table and learn why these grouping elements matter for styling, scrolling and printing.
lessons.goal: Upgrade a flat table into a fully structured one: titled, banded into head/body/foot, with columns addressable via colgroup.
lessons.whyItMatters: Production tables are rarely four rows of demo data — they are long, scrollable, printable reports. The structural elements in this lesson are what make those behaviours possible: sticky header rows need a thead to pin, printed reports repeat thead on every page, totals live in tfoot, and column-wide styling hangs off colgroup. Skipping them works for toy tables and collapses the moment requirements grow.
steps: Read about caption and why a table should announce its own subject.
Study the three row bands — thead, tbody, tfoot — and what each contains.
Read why the grouping matters: scrolling, printing and styling all depend on it.
Learn colgroup and col, including the span attribute.
Open the starter code: a flat expenses table with no structure.
Complete tasks 1–6, adding each structural element, and run the checks.

lessons.explanation: caption names the table and must be the first child of table. colgroup comes next and describes the vertical structure the row markup cannot express: here one plain column and a col spanning the two amount columns, giving CSS a single hook for both. thead holds the header row, tbody the data, tfoot the totals — three bands the browser can treat differently when scrolling or printing. Note that tfoot renders at the bottom regardless, and every row still lives inside one of the three bands.
lessons.example:
A finance page shows a 200-row expense report. Without structure, scrolling loses the header immediately and printing repeats nothing, so page four is a sea of unlabeled numbers.

With thead/tbody/tfoot in place, CSS pins the header while tbody scrolls, print engines repeat the head on every sheet, and the totals row stays visually anchored at the bottom — all without a single line of JavaScript.

commonMistakes: Placing caption anywhere but first. The caption element must be the first child of table or the document is invalid.
Putting the totals row at the end of tbody instead of in tfoot. It renders in the same place, but loses its meaning and its print/scroll behaviour.
Expecting colgroup to carry any styling by default — col elements accept only a handful of CSS properties (background, width, border, visibility), so test what you hang on them.
Forgetting that browsers auto-generate a tbody around stray rows. Your CSS selectors like table > tr silently fail because the tr is actually inside an implicit tbody.
lessons.proTip: Inspect any table in DevTools and you will see a tbody you may never have written — the parser inserts one automatically. Write it explicitly anyway: what is visible in your source is what your teammates can reason about.

coding.intro: You will take a flat expenses table and add every structural element: caption, colgroup/col, thead, tbody and tfoot.

sections.heading: caption: the table's own title
sections.body:
A caption is the accessible name of a table — a short phrase stating what the data is. It must be the very first child of the table element, before any rows or groups, and each table can have at most one.

By default the caption renders as a line of text above the table (CSS caption-side can move it below). More importantly, screen readers announce it when a user enters the table, and it is what appears when tables are listed for navigation. A page with three tables named 'Monthly expenses', 'Annual summary' and 'Payment schedule' is navigable; three anonymous tables are not.

Prefer caption over a nearby heading when the title belongs to the table itself: the association is explicit in markup, travels with the table if it moves, and does not add noise to the page's heading outline.
sections.code: Monthly expenses, first term 2026

sections.heading: thead, tbody, tfoot: three named bands
sections.body:
Rows can be grouped into three horizontal bands. thead holds the rows that label the columns — usually one row of th elements. tbody holds the actual data rows. tfoot holds summary rows: totals, averages, footnote rows.

The required order in source is thead, then tbody, then tfoot (older HTML allowed tfoot before tbody; modern HTML does not). Regardless of source order, browsers always render tfoot at the visual bottom.

One behaviour surprises everyone eventually: tbody exists even when you never wrote it. The HTML parser wraps any bare rows in an implicit tbody, so document.querySelector('table > tr') finds nothing and CSS child selectors behave unexpectedly. Writing tbody explicitly costs one line and removes the surprise.

MonthRent
January800
Total800

sections.heading: Why the grouping matters
sections.body:
The bands are not bureaucracy — three real behaviours hang off them.

Scrolling: a long table inside a fixed-height container can keep its header visible while the data scrolls. The standard technique — position: sticky on the thead cells — needs a thead to target. Without the band, there is nothing to pin.

Printing: when a multi-page table is printed, browsers repeat the thead rows at the top of every printed page and can repeat tfoot at the bottom. A 40-page report whose column labels appear only on page one is the direct cost of skipping thead.

Styling and scripting: the bands are clean hooks. tbody tr:nth-child(odd) stripes only data rows without accidentally striping the header; a script that sorts rows can rebuild tbody alone and leave head and foot untouched.

sections.heading: colgroup and col: talking about columns
sections.body:
Table markup is row-major, so there is no element that contains a column's cells. colgroup and col exist to fix that for the cases where you need to address columns anyway. colgroup sits immediately after caption (before any rows) and contains col elements, one per column, in left-to-right order.

A col with span="2" stands for two adjacent columns at once — handy when several columns share a role, like a pair of amount columns that should share a background and width. Note this span attribute is about column description; it is unrelated to the cell-merging colspan you will meet in the next lesson.

col elements are empty and accept only a limited set of CSS properties — background-color, width, border and visibility are the reliable ones. Text styling like color or font-weight does not work through col; for that you style the cells themselves. Within its limits, colgroup saves you from repeating a class on every cell of a column.
sections.code: Monthly expenses

sections.heading: Multiple tbody: grouping rows by theme
sections.body:
A table may contain more than one tbody, and this is the idiomatic way to group related runs of rows: quarters within a year, teams within a league, categories within a price list.

Each tbody is a styling and scripting unit. You can give alternating groups different backgrounds, add a visual gap between groups with border-spacing tricks, collapse or expand one group with a single class toggle, or re-sort rows within their group only. Screen-reader support for announcing row groups is limited, so if group identity matters to understanding the data, also give each group a labelling row (a th spanning the table works well, using techniques from the next lesson).

The alternative people reach for — separate tables per group — costs you shared column widths and a single caption. Multiple tbody keeps one table, one grid, one set of headers.

sections.heading: The full ordering, once and for all
sections.body:
A completely structured table has a fixed internal order: caption first, then colgroup, then thead, then one or more tbody elements, then tfoot. Nothing else sits directly inside table, and every row lives inside one of the three band elements.

You will not need every part in every table — a four-row table with no totals can be caption + thead + tbody and nothing else. The skill is knowing the full menu so that when a requirement lands ('make the header sticky', 'print with repeated headings', 'shade the amount columns') you already have the element it attaches to.

The starter table in the editor has none of this: bare rows, a heading floating above it, totals mixed into the data. Restore the order piece by piece as the tasks direct.

lessons.title: Merge table cells with colspan and rowspan — and keep them accessible
lessons.summary: Span cells across columns and rows, plan the grid so every row still adds up, and wire up complex-table accessibility with scope and headers/id.
lessons.goal: Build a two-level sales table using colspan and rowspan, with every cell's meaning preserved for assistive technology.
lessons.whyItMatters: Merged cells appear in nearly every real report: grouped column headings, category labels spanning several rows, summary cells. Spanning is also where tables most often break — one miscounted cell shears the whole grid — and where accessibility quietly dies, because a screen reader can no longer infer which headers describe which cell. This lesson teaches both halves: making the numbers add up and making the relationships explicit.
steps: Read how colspan and rowspan consume grid positions.
Work through the planning section — draw the grid before writing any spans.
Read the four scope values, including rowgroup and colgroup for spanned headers.
Study the headers/id technique for tables too complex for scope alone.
Open the starter code and add the spans (tasks 1–2), row headers (task 3) and scope/headers wiring (tasks 4–5).
Run the checks and confirm the grid renders without gaps or overhangs.

Q1 Q2
North 12 15
lessons.explanation: The table is three columns wide. In the first row, the Region header spends a rowspan to cover two rows, and Half 1 spends a colspan to cover two columns — together they fill all three positions. The second row supplies only Q1 and Q2 because column one is already occupied from above. Half 1 spans a group of columns, so its scope is colgroup rather than col. The headers attribute on each data cell then lists the ids of every header that applies to it, making the cell's full meaning explicit no matter how tangled the geometry.
lessons.example:
Picture the grid as graph paper three squares wide. Every cell you write claims the next free square in its row; a colspan claims extra squares to the right, a rowspan reserves the same square in rows below.

Write 'Region' with rowspan 2 and square one of row two is pre-claimed — so row two only needs two more cells, not three. Miss that and Q2 overhangs the table edge: the classic spanning bug, visible as a lonely cell jutting out.

lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a clean two-tier header — Region on the left spanning both header rows, Half 1 bridging Q1 and Q2 — above two aligned data rows, with no cell overhanging the grid.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to remove cells swallowed by a span. A rowspan reserves space in following rows, so those rows must contain fewer cells — writing the full count shears the grid.
Counting a colspan cell as one column when checking row widths. A colspan="2" cell occupies two positions; each row's spans plus plain cells must total the table's column count.
Using scope="col" on a header that spans several columns. A multi-column header labels a group, so it takes scope="colgroup" (and a multi-row header takes rowgroup).
Leaving headers/id half-wired: ids on the th elements but stale or missing id lists in the headers attributes. Every id referenced must exist, and the list must cover all applicable headers.
lessons.proTip: Before writing any spanned table, sketch it on paper and number the columns. Then for each tr, add up plain cells plus colspans plus positions reserved by rowspans from above — every row must reach the same total. Thirty seconds of arithmetic saves an hour of tag shuffling.

sections.heading: colspan: one cell across several columns
sections.body:
The colspan attribute makes a single cell occupy that many column positions in its row. colspan="2" on a th means the cell stretches over two columns; the row then needs correspondingly fewer cells to reach the table's width.

The classic use is a group heading over related columns: 'Half 1' bridging Q1 and Q2, 'Contact' bridging Phone and Email. The grouped heading sits in an upper header row; the individual column headings sit in the row below it.

colspan applies to td as well as th — a data cell can span, which is how you build full-width divider rows or notes inside a table. The value must be a positive whole number; a colspan larger than the space remaining in the row does not widen the table, browsers simply clamp it, so oversized values are bugs waiting to confuse someone.
sections.code:
<tr>
  <th colspan="2">Half 1</th>
</tr>
<tr>
  <th>Q1</th>
  <th>Q2</th>
</tr>

sections.heading: rowspan: one cell down several rows
sections.body:
rowspan is the vertical twin: the cell claims its column position in this row and reserves the same position in the next rows down. rowspan="2" on the Region header means the cell exists in both header rows, sitting vertically centred across them by default.

The crucial mechanical consequence: the rows below a rowspan must omit the cell for that column. The position is already taken; supplying a cell anyway pushes everything rightward and the row overhangs the grid. This is the single most common spanning bug, and it looks exactly like 'my table has a random extra cell sticking out'.

Typical rowspan uses: a corner header covering a two-row header block, a category label beside the rows in that category ('Beverages' next to three drink rows), or a merged cell for repeated values.
sections.code:
<tr>
  <th rowspan="2">Region</th>
  <th colspan="2">Half 1</th>
</tr>
<tr>
  <!-- no first cell: Region occupies it from above -->
  <th>Q1</th>
  <th>Q2</th>
</tr>

sections.heading: Planning the grid so the counts add up
sections.body:
Spanned tables reward five minutes of planning. Start by fixing the total column count — the widest row defines it. Our sales table is three columns: Region, Q1, Q2.

Now audit each row. Row one: Region (1 position, plus a reservation below) + Half 1 (2 positions via colspan) = 3. Correct. Row two: 1 position pre-claimed by Region's rowspan + Q1 + Q2 = 3. Correct — so we write only two cells. Data rows: a row header plus two data cells = 3.

Do this audit whenever you add or remove a span, because spans interact: a change in one row silently changes how many cells its neighbours need. If the rendered table shows a hole, a row is short; if a cell juts out past the right edge, a row is over — usually because a rowspan's reservation was forgotten.
sections.code:
<!-- Column audit, 3 columns total:
 row 1: Region(1, spans down) + Half 1(2) = 3
 row 2: [reserved](1) + Q1(1) + Q2(1)   = 3
 row 3: North(1) + 12(1) + 15(1)        = 3
-->

sections.heading: The four scope values
sections.body:
You already use scope="col" and scope="row". Spanned headers need the other two values, because a merged header labels a group of columns or rows, not a single one.

scope="colgroup" goes on a header spanning multiple columns: Half 1 describes both the Q1 and Q2 columns, so every cell in either column inherits it as context. scope="rowgroup" is the mirror for a header spanning multiple rows — a 'Beverages' label with rowspan="3" scoped as rowgroup applies to all three drink rows.

With all four values placed correctly, a screen reader arriving at the number 15 can announce 'North, Half 1, Q2: 15' — the complete address of the cell. That is the standard to aim for: every data cell in a complex table should have an unambiguous, machine-derivable set of headers.
sections.code:
<th rowspan="2" scope="col">Region</th>
<th colspan="2" scope="colgroup">Half 1</th>
<th scope="col">Q1</th>
<th scope="row">North</th>

sections.heading: headers and id: explicit wiring for hard cases
sections.body:
Some tables outgrow what scope can express — multiple stacked header layers, irregular blocks, headers that apply non-contiguously. For these, HTML offers a fully explicit mechanism: give each header cell an id, and give each data cell a headers attribute listing the ids of every header that describes it, separated by spaces.

The browser then has zero guessing to do: the cell declares its own context. The cost is verbosity and maintenance — every table edit must keep the id lists truthful, and a typo in one id silently breaks the association since nothing validates it for you.

Practical guidance: use scope alone for anything scope can describe, which is most tables, including the one in this lesson. Reach for headers/id when scope genuinely cannot express the relationships — and once you commit to it, wire every data cell, not just some, so the table behaves consistently. In this exercise you will apply it alongside scope to see the mechanics.
sections.code: North 12 15

sections.heading: Knowing when to simplify instead
sections.body:
The final skill with complex tables is recognising when not to build one. Every span you add raises the cost of reading, maintaining and navigating the table. Before merging, ask whether the structure serves the data or just imitates a spreadsheet someone exported.

Often a monster table splits cleanly into two simple ones — one per half-year, say — each covered by plain scope="col" and scope="row", with a caption distinguishing them. Screen-reader users, mobile layouts and future maintainers all benefit, and you drop the headers/id bookkeeping entirely.

When the merged structure genuinely is the data — grouped quarters under halves, categories spanning rows — use the tools from this lesson without apology. The goal is the simplest table that tells the truth about the data, spanned or not.

lessons.title: Send data to a server with your first working forms
lessons.summary: Understand what a form submission really is: the form element, action, GET vs POST, the name attribute as the key of every value, and enctype.
lessons.goal: Build two working forms — a POST signup and a GET search — and know exactly what data leaves the browser when each is submitted.
lessons.whyItMatters: Forms are how the web collects data: logins, checkouts, searches, uploads. Most form bugs in real projects are not visual — they are fields that never arrive at the server because a name was missing, passwords leaking into URLs because the method was GET, or file uploads arriving empty because enctype was wrong. Understanding what a submission actually sends makes all three bugs impossible.
steps: Read what happens at the moment a form is submitted.
Study action, then the GET vs POST comparison — including what each does to the URL.
Read the section on name carefully: it decides what data exists in the submission at all.
Skim the enctype section so file uploads never surprise you later.
In the editor, complete the signup form (tasks 1–4), then the search form (task 5).
Run the checks and trace mentally what each form would send.
lessons.prompt:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="text" id="email" name="email">
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

<!-- Submitting with 'ana@example.com' typed in sends:
     POST /subscribe
     body: email=ana%40example.com -->
lessons.explanation: On submit, the browser walks the form, collects every control that has a name, and builds name=value pairs from them — here just email=ana@example.com, encoded for transport. action says which URL receives the pairs and method says how they travel: POST puts them in the request body, keeping them out of the address bar. The button of type submit is the trigger; without any submit control the form can only be submitted by pressing Enter in a text field.
lessons.example:
Type 'coffee' into a GET search form named q and submit: the browser navigates to /search?q=coffee. The data is the URL — visible, bookmarkable, shareable, stored in history.

Submit the same value through a POST form and the URL stays clean (/search); the pair q=coffee travels inside the request body instead. Same data, different envelope — and that difference is the entire GET vs POST decision.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, finish the newsletter signup form: point it at /subscribe with method POST, name the email field so its value is actually sent, and add a submit button. Then build the small GET search form below it.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a signup form with a labelled email field and Subscribe button, plus a one-field search form. All five checks pass; submitting would send email=... via POST and q=... via GET respectively.
commonMistakes: Omitting name on an input. A control without a name contributes nothing to the submission — the field silently vanishes from the data.
Sending sensitive data with GET. Values in a query string end up in browser history, server logs and shared links; anything private travels by POST.
Confusing name with id. id is for labels, CSS and scripts inside the page; name is the key the server receives. A field usually needs both, doing different jobs.
Setting enctype="multipart/form-data" only after noticing file uploads arrive empty. Any form containing a file input needs it from the start, together with method POST.
lessons.proTip: Open DevTools' Network tab, submit any form, and click the request: you can read exactly which name=value pairs left the browser and whether they rode in the URL or the body. It is the fastest way to debug 'the server never got my field'.

coding.intro: You will complete a POST newsletter signup and build a GET search form, learning exactly what each submission puts on the wire.

sections.heading: What a form actually does
sections.body:
A form is a machine for turning typed input into an HTTP request. The form element itself is invisible — it draws nothing. Its job is to group controls (inputs, buttons, and later selects and textareas) and define what happens when the user submits.

At the moment of submission, the browser performs three steps: it collects every control inside the form that has a name attribute, builds a list of name=value pairs from their current values, and sends that list to a URL. The page then navigates to the server's response.

Everything else in forms — methods, encodings, buttons — is configuration of those three steps. Keep the model in mind and the attributes stop being trivia: action configures where the pairs go, method configures how they travel, enctype configures how they are packaged, and name decides which pairs exist at all.
sections.code:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <!-- controls live here -->
</form>

sections.heading: action: where the data goes
sections.body:
The action attribute holds the URL that will receive the submission. It can be a relative path like /subscribe, handled by your own server, or an absolute URL on another origin. When the form is submitted, the browser sends the collected data there and displays whatever comes back — a thank-you page, search results, a validation error.

If you omit action entirely, the form submits to the current page's own URL. You will see this on pages that both display a form and process it. An empty action="" historically meant the same thing but is technically invalid HTML — either provide a real URL or leave the attribute off.

One mental adjustment matters here: plain HTML form submission is a full page navigation, exactly like clicking a link. The 'submit without reloading' behaviour you know from modern apps is JavaScript intercepting the form — a later layer built on top of what you are learning now.
sections.code:
<!-- Sends the data to /subscribe on the same site -->
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">...</form>

<!-- No action: submits to the current URL -->
<form method="post">...</form>

sections.heading: GET vs POST: two ways to travel
sections.body:
The method attribute chooses between two transports. method="get" (the default when omitted) appends the data to the action URL as a query string: /search?q=coffee&page=2. method="post" sends the data in the body of the request, leaving the URL untouched.

Because GET puts data in the URL, the resulting page is bookmarkable and shareable — reload it, and the same submission happens again harmlessly. That fits requests that only read data: searches, filters, sorting, pagination. The costs of the same property: values are visible in the address bar, saved in history, and logged by servers; URLs also have practical length limits.

POST keeps data out of the URL and is the right method for anything that changes state or carries private values: registrations, logins, payments, uploads, deletions. Browsers even warn before re-submitting a POST on refresh, precisely because repeating it might repeat a real-world effect.

The rule of thumb: GET to ask, POST to act. And never GET for secrets — a password in a query string is a password in every log file along the way.
sections.code:
<!-- GET: data becomes part of the URL -->
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input type="text" name="q">
</form>
<!-- → /search?q=coffee -->

<!-- POST: data rides in the request body -->
<form action="/signup" method="post">...</form>

sections.heading: name: the key of every value
sections.body:
The name attribute is the single most important attribute in forms, because it is the key under which a control's value is submitted. An input with name="email" containing 'ana@example.com' contributes the pair email=ana@example.com. An input with no name contributes nothing — the browser skips it entirely, no matter what the user typed.

This is the number one forms bug in practice: a beautifully styled field whose value never reaches the server. The field had an id, a label, a placeholder — everything except a name. Remember the division of labour: id identifies the element inside the page (for label pairing, CSS, scripts); name identifies the value inside the submission. Servers read names, never ids.

What gets sent is always the current value at submit time: whatever text is in the box, or for choice controls (next lessons) the value attribute of the selected option. Special characters are percent-encoded for transport — @ becomes %40 — and the server framework decodes them back automatically.
sections.code:
<!-- Sent as email=... -->
<input type="text" id="email" name="email">

<!-- Never sent: no name -->
<input type="text" id="nickname">

sections.heading: enctype: how the payload is packaged
sections.body:
For POST forms, the enctype attribute chooses the packaging format of the body. The default, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, writes all pairs in one string — name=value&name2=value2, percent-encoded — and is right for any form made of text-like values.

The important alternative is multipart/form-data. It splits the body into separate parts, one per field, each with its own small header — which is the only format that can carry file contents. Any form containing <input type="file"> must declare method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data", or the server receives just the file's name as text instead of the file itself. This is worth memorising now, before the file-input lesson, because the failure is silent.

A third value, text/plain, exists for historical reasons and sends loosely formatted text no server should be asked to parse reliably. Treat it as trivia. GET forms ignore enctype entirely — their data always goes URL-style into the query string.
sections.code:
<!-- Default: fine for text fields -->
<form action="/signup" method="post">...</form>

<!-- Required as soon as a file input exists -->
<form action="/upload" method="post"
      enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <input type="file" name="avatar">
</form>

sections.heading: A first working form, assembled
sections.body:
Combine the pieces and a minimal real form emerges: a form with action and method, one named text input with a label, and a submit button. That is genuinely everything a server needs to receive data from a user.

Trace a submission through it. The user types ana@example.com and clicks Subscribe. The browser finds the named controls — just email — builds email=ana%40example.com, and because the method is post, sends it in the body of a request to /subscribe. The server reads the email key, stores the address, and responds with a confirmation page the browser then displays.

In the editor you will build exactly this, plus a GET search form so you use both methods deliberately. Every later forms lesson — labels, choice inputs, specialised types — only adds richer controls into this same submission machine.
sections.code:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="text" id="email" name="email">
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>

lessons.title: Pair every input with a real label and pick the right button
lessons.summary: Master label/for/id pairing, the core text-like inputs, why placeholder is not a label, and the button element's default-type trap.
lessons.goal: Build a login form where every field has a programmatically linked label and every button has an explicit, correct type.
lessons.whyItMatters: Unlabeled inputs are among the most common accessibility failures on the web, and they hurt everyone: screen readers announce an anonymous 'edit text', mobile users miss the enlarged tap target, and autofill guesses wrong. Meanwhile the button default-type trap — a plain button inside a form submitting it by surprise — is a real bug class that breaks 'Show password' toggles and delete confirmations in production apps.
steps: Read how label works and what the for/id pairing gives users.
Compare the wrapping alternative and when to use each style.
Review the text-like inputs and the difference between value, name and placeholder.
Read the button section — especially the default type=submit pitfall.
In the editor, label both fields (tasks 1–3), then fix the buttons (tasks 4–5).
Run the checks, then click each label in the preview and watch focus jump to its field.
lessons.prompt:
<label for="username">Username</label>
<input type="text" id="username" name="username">

<label for="password">Password</label>
<input type="password" id="password" name="password">

<button type="submit">Log in</button>
<button type="button">Show password</button>
lessons.explanation: Each label's for attribute holds exactly the id of its input, forging a programmatic link: clicking the label focuses the field, and assistive technology announces the label text when the field gains focus. The password input masks what is typed but still submits under its name like any field. Both buttons declare their type explicitly — the first submits the form, while the second is inert to submission, existing purely for a script to hook onto; without type="button" it would silently submit the form too.
lessons.example:
A user with a motor impairment tries to tap a bare 10-pixel checkbox and misses repeatedly. With a paired label, the entire text 'Remember me' becomes the tap target and the first tap lands.

A screen-reader user tabs into an unlabeled field and hears only 'edit text'. Password? Email? Search? With for/id pairing they hear 'Username, edit text' — the field explains itself.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, wire the login form: link both labels with matching for/id pairs, make the password field a real password input, give the login button an explicit submit type, and defuse the Show-password button with type="button".
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a login form where clicking either label focuses its field, typing in the password field shows dots, and the Show password button no longer submits the form when clicked.
commonMistakes: Relying on placeholder as the field's only label. The hint disappears on first keystroke, is skipped by many assistive setups, and its low-contrast text fails users with poor vision.
Mismatched for/id pairs — a for pointing at a name, a typo, or a duplicated id. The link fails silently; always click the label to verify focus moves.
Writing <button> inside a form without a type. Its default is submit, so a decorative or JS-only button unexpectedly submits the whole form.
Adding a reset button by habit. Users click it by accident and lose everything they typed; genuine use cases for reset are rare.
lessons.proTip: A quick audit for any form: click every label — focus must land in a field; then tab through and confirm each field is announced by name. Two minutes, and it catches the majority of labelling bugs before any user does.

sections.heading: label: the clickable name of a field
sections.body:
Every input needs a visible name a human can read, and HTML has a dedicated element for it: label. The pairing mechanism is explicit — the input carries an id, and the label carries a for attribute containing exactly that id.

The pairing buys three behaviours. Clicking or tapping the label focuses (or toggles) the field, dramatically enlarging the hit area — decisive on touch screens and for anyone with imprecise motor control. Screen readers announce the label text when the field receives focus, turning 'edit text' into 'Username, edit text'. And browsers use label text as a signal for autofill.

The pairing is exact and case-sensitive: for must match an id, not a name, and that id must be unique in the document. If two elements share the id, the label binds to the first and your form misbehaves subtly. Nothing warns you when a pairing is broken — the form just silently loses all three behaviours, which is why the click-the-label test belongs in your routine.
sections.code:
<label for="username">Username</label>
<input type="text" id="username" name="username">

sections.heading: The wrapping alternative
sections.body:
There is a second, equally valid pairing style: put the input inside the label element. The association is then implicit — no for or id needed for the link — and the entire wrapped area, text included, becomes clickable.

Wrapping shines for checkboxes and radio buttons, where the tiny control and its text naturally read as one unit. The for/id style shines when layout separates label and field — labels in one grid column, inputs in another — or when styling needs them as independent elements.

Two cautions. First, choose one mechanism per field; using both (wrapping and for/id) is allowed only if the for points at the wrapped input, and it adds nothing. Second, some assistive technology historically handled explicit for/id more reliably, so many teams standardise on it for text fields and allow wrapping for choice controls. Either way: every input gets exactly one label, and no label goes empty.
sections.code:
<!-- Implicit pairing: input nested in label -->
<label>
  <input type="checkbox" name="remember">
  Remember me
</label>

sections.heading: The text-like inputs: text and password
sections.body:
input type="text" is the general single-line field, and the default if type is missing or misspelled — worth knowing, because a typo like type="pasword" silently produces a plain text field.

input type="password" behaves identically in submission terms but masks the display with dots. Understand what it does and does not protect: it hides the value from someone looking over the user's shoulder, and browsers block copying it. It does not encrypt anything — the value travels like any other field, which is why password forms must POST and sites must use HTTPS.

Three attributes complete the picture. name, as always, is the submission key. value sets the initial content of the field — what is pre-filled when the page loads, and what the user edits; the submitted value is whatever the field holds at submit time. maxlength caps input length — fine as a convenience, never as security, since anyone can bypass client-side limits.
sections.code:
<input type="text" id="username" name="username" value="ana">
<input type="password" id="password" name="password" maxlength="64">

sections.heading: placeholder is not a label
sections.body:
The placeholder attribute shows dimmed hint text inside an empty field. Its legitimate job is a format example: a date field hinting 'DD/MM/YYYY', a phone field hinting '+30 210 ...'.

Using placeholder as the field's only label is a design pattern you will see everywhere, and it fails users in stacked ways. The text vanishes the moment typing starts, so users mid-form can no longer see what the field asks for — and neither can anyone reviewing their answers before submitting. The default grey typically fails contrast requirements. Some assistive technologies do not read placeholders at all. And because the hint sits where the value goes, users can mistake a placeholder for pre-filled content and skip the field.

The rule: every field gets a real label, and placeholder is an optional extra hint — never load-bearing. If a design insists on the floating-hint look, implement it with a real label element positioned by CSS, keeping the accessibility intact.
sections.code:
<!-- Wrong: hint doing a label's job -->
<input type="text" name="email" placeholder="Email">

<!-- Right: label + optional format hint -->
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="text" id="email" name="email"
       placeholder="you@example.com">

sections.heading: The three input buttons
sections.body:
Before the button element, forms used input for buttons, and you will still meet all three kinds. input type="submit" renders a button that submits the form; its value attribute is its visible text. input type="reset" clears every field back to its initial values. input type="button" does nothing on its own — a bare hook for JavaScript.

Two practical notes. A submit control also matters for keyboard flow: pressing Enter in a text field submits the form via it. And reset deserves suspicion — users hit it while aiming for submit and watch their work evaporate; include it only when clearing a form is a genuine, common need.

These input buttons are void elements: their text can only be plain value text, which is the main reason the button element has largely replaced them.
sections.code:
<input type="submit" value="Log in">
<input type="reset" value="Clear">
<input type="button" value="Show password">

sections.heading: The button element and its default-type trap
sections.body:
button is the modern button: a real container element, so it can hold formatted text, icons or images, and it is easier to style. It takes the same three types as its input ancestors: submit, reset and button.

Here is the trap that catches even experienced developers: inside a form, a button with no type attribute defaults to type="submit". You add a harmless 'Show password' toggle, wire it to JavaScript, and every click also submits the form — the page navigates away, the form data flies to the server, and the bug report says 'clicking the eye icon logs me out'.

The professional habit is to always write the type explicitly on every button element: type="submit" for the one control meant to send the form, type="button" for everything wired to scripts. Outside a form the default is effectively inert, but the habit costs nothing and makes intent readable. One more capability worth knowing: a button can carry its own name and value, which are submitted only when that specific button triggers the submission — the classic way to distinguish 'Save' from 'Save and publish' server-side.
sections.code:
<!-- The one that submits -->
<button type="submit">Log in</button>

<!-- Inert to submission; JavaScript's hook -->
<button type="button">Show password</button>

lessons.title: Offer choices with radio groups, checkboxes and fieldsets
lessons.summary: Build single-choice radio groups and multi-choice checkbox sets, preselect defaults, and group them accessibly with fieldset and legend.
lessons.goal: Build a pizza order form with a correctly grouped radio set, a checkbox set, a preselected default, and a label on every choice.
lessons.whyItMatters: Choice controls carry the highest-stakes data in most products — plan selection, consent boxes, configuration options. They are also where three silent bugs cluster: radios that do not exclude each other because their names differ, submissions that send meaningless values because value was omitted, and choice groups whose shared question is invisible to screen readers because there is no fieldset. This lesson closes all three.
steps: Read how a shared name turns individual radios into one exclusive group.
Study value and checked — what is sent, and how defaults are declared.
Read the two checkbox patterns: single boolean and multi-select group.
Learn what fieldset and legend add for grouped choices.
In the editor, build the size radios (tasks 1–2), the toppings checkboxes (task 3) and the fieldsets (task 4), labelling everything (task 5).
Run the checks, then click each option's text and watch the control toggle.
lessons.prompt:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Size</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="size" value="small"> Small</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="size" value="medium" checked> Medium</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="size" value="large"> Large</label>
</fieldset>
lessons.explanation: All three radios share name="size", which is what makes them one group: selecting any of them deselects the others, and on submit exactly one pair like size=medium is sent. Each radio carries a value, because that value — not the visible text — is what the server receives. checked on the middle option preselects it, so the group can never submit empty. The fieldset draws the options together and its legend states the question they answer, which screen readers announce alongside each option's own label.
lessons.example:
Ask 'what size pizza?' with three radios named size1, size2 and size3, and users can select all three at once — three groups of one instead of one group of three. The form looks right and behaves absurdly.

Rename them all to size and the browser enforces the either/or for you. That is the entire radio contract: grouping is by name, never by proximity in the markup.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete the order form: three size radios sharing one name with Medium preselected, at least two topping checkboxes sharing the name topping, each set wrapped in a fieldset with a legend, and every single option labelled.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows two boxed groups — Size with Medium already selected, Toppings with none — where clicking any option's text toggles it, and only one size can ever be active.
commonMistakes: Giving radios in one group different names. Exclusivity comes only from the shared name; differing names create independent one-button groups.
Omitting value on radios and checkboxes. The server then receives the default 'on' for whichever was chosen — size=on says nothing about which size.
Preselecting nothing in a radio group. Once a radio group is touched it cannot be fully deselected, but an untouched group submits nothing — pick a sensible default with checked.
Skipping fieldset for grouped choices. Each radio's own label says 'Medium', but only a legend tells assistive technology what question 'Medium' answers.
lessons.proTip: checked="checked", checked="", and bare checked are all identical — it is a boolean attribute, so its presence is the whole message. The same is true of disabled, required and readonly; write the bare form and never write checked="false", which still checks the box.

coding.intro: You will build the choice controls of a pizza order form: an exclusive size group, a multi-select toppings group, and accessible grouping around both.

sections.heading: Radio buttons: one of many
sections.body:
A radio button offers one option from a mutually exclusive set — named after the mechanical station buttons on old radios, where pressing one popped the others out. In HTML each option is its own input type="radio", and the grouping mechanism is subtle but absolute: radios belong to the same group if and only if they share the same name attribute within the same form.

Position means nothing. Three radios can sit in different corners of the form and still be one group if their names match; three adjacent radios with different names are three unrelated groups. When a user picks one member of a group, the browser deselects whichever other member was active.

On submission the group contributes at most one pair: its shared name with the chosen option's value. If no option is selected, the group contributes nothing at all — not an empty value, simply absence — which is a classic source of server-side 'missing field' surprises.
sections.code:
<input type="radio" name="size" value="small">
<input type="radio" name="size" value="medium">
<input type="radio" name="size" value="large">
<!-- one group, because one shared name -->

sections.heading: value: what the server actually receives
sections.body:
The text a user reads next to a radio lives in its label. The data the server receives lives in the value attribute. These are deliberately separate: the label can say 'Large (+2.50 €)' while the value stays a clean machine token like large.

Forgetting value has a specific, confusing failure mode: a selected control with no value submits the literal string 'on'. Your server then receives size=on — it knows a size was chosen but not which. Because the form still 'works', this bug routinely survives until someone reads the stored data.

Give every radio and checkbox an explicit value, and keep values stable and code-like (lowercase, no spaces) even when labels are wordy or translated. The label is for humans and may change freely; the value is an API contract with the server and should not.
sections.code:
<label>
  <input type="radio" name="size" value="large">
  Large (+2.50 €)
</label>
<!-- submits: size=large -->

sections.heading: checked: declaring the default
sections.body:
The checked attribute preselects a control when the page loads. It is a boolean attribute: its mere presence checks the control, regardless of any value you assign it — even checked="false" checks the box, a trap worth seeing once so you never fall into it.

For radio groups, a sensible default is more than politeness. An untouched radio group submits nothing, and a touched one can never return to fully unselected — the user can change the choice but not unmake it. Preselecting the most common option with checked gives every submission a value and shows users what a valid answer looks like. Put checked on exactly one member per group; if you mark several, the last one wins.

The attribute defines the initial state, not the live one. After the user interacts, the current selection is what submits — the markup's checked is only where things started.
sections.code:
<label>
  <input type="radio" name="size" value="medium" checked>
  Medium
</label>

sections.heading: Checkboxes alone: a yes or no
sections.body:
A single input type="checkbox" represents an independent boolean: newsletter opt-in, accept-the-terms, remember-me. Unlike radios, a checkbox can always be freely toggled off again — it answers its own yes/no question and belongs to no exclusive group.

Its submission behaviour is the part that surprises people. Checked: the pair name=value is sent (or name=on if you set no value). Unchecked: nothing is sent — the name is entirely absent from the submission. Servers must therefore treat 'key missing' as the false state; there is no terms=false coming to help you.

A checkbox can also carry checked to start ticked. Legal note from practice: pre-ticking consent boxes (marketing emails, data sharing) is prohibited by regulations like GDPR — consent must be an action, not an omission. Default states are a design and compliance decision, not just a technical one.
sections.code:
<label>
  <input type="checkbox" name="terms" value="accepted">
  I accept the terms
</label>
<!-- checked → terms=accepted ; unchecked → nothing sent -->

sections.heading: Checkbox groups: several of many
sections.body:
For 'choose any that apply' questions, use several checkboxes sharing one name, each with its own value — structurally like a radio group, but without exclusivity. A user picking mushrooms and olives submits two pairs under the same key: topping=mushrooms and topping=olives.

Repeated keys are legal and standard in form data; every server framework offers a way to read all values for a key as a list (some conventions, like PHP's, expect the name written as topping[] — follow your backend's convention). The browser sends the chosen pairs in document order.

Decide between the two group types by the question's grammar: 'pick one' is radios, 'pick any' is checkboxes. Users have deep muscle memory for the visual difference — circles mean exclusive, squares mean multiple — which is one more reason never to restyle one to look like the other.
sections.code:
<label><input type="checkbox" name="topping" value="mushrooms"> Mushrooms</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="topping" value="olives"> Olives</label>
<label><input type="checkbox" name="topping" value="peppers"> Peppers</label>
<!-- picking two → topping=mushrooms&topping=olives -->

sections.heading: fieldset and legend: naming the question
sections.body:
Each individual option has a label, but the question the options answer — Size? Toppings? — lives nowhere unless you give it a home. That home is fieldset, a grouping element for related controls, with legend as its first child stating the group's purpose.

The accessibility payoff is concrete: when a screen-reader user reaches an option, the legend is announced together with the option's label — 'Size, Medium, radio button' — so the choice is never context-free. Visually, browsers draw a thin border around a fieldset with the legend breaking the border line; keep or restyle it with CSS as you wish, but keep the elements.

Use a fieldset for every radio group and every checkbox group, and for larger logical regions of long forms (shipping address vs billing address). One more capability: disabled on a fieldset disables every control inside it at once — handy for switching off a whole section until an earlier answer makes it relevant.
sections.code:
<fieldset>
  <legend>Toppings</legend>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="topping" value="mushrooms"> Mushrooms</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="topping" value="olives"> Olives</label>
</fieldset>
