lessons.title: Use the specialised input types: email, number, range, color, file, hidden
lessons.summary: Swap generic text fields for inputs with built-in meaning — validation, the right mobile keyboard, native pickers — plus number constraints, file uploads and hidden data.
lessons.goal: Build a product review form using the specialised input types with their constraint attributes, a scoped file upload, and a hidden field.
lessons.whyItMatters: Choosing the precise input type is free quality: email fields get the @ keyboard on phones and basic validation without a line of JavaScript, number fields reject letters, range gives you a native slider, and file inputs handle the OS picker for you. Teams that leave everything as type="text" end up re-implementing all of this by hand — worse, and at cost. Hidden inputs, meanwhile, are how real forms carry context like record ids through a submission.
steps: Read the text-like family — email, url, tel, search — and what each changes.
Study number and its min/max/step constraint attributes.
Read range and how an output element pairs with it, then color.
Read file carefully: accept, multiple, and the enctype requirement.
Read hidden and its legitimate uses.
In the editor, complete tasks 1–5, then run the checks and try each control in the preview.
lessons.prompt:
<input type="email" name="email">
<input type="number" name="rating" min="1" max="10" step="1">
<input type="range" name="sweetness" min="0" max="100" value="50">
<input type="color" name="accent" value="#336699">
<input type="file" name="photo" accept="image/*" multiple>
<input type="hidden" name="product-id" value="prod-8841">
lessons.explanation: Each line replaces a generic text box with a control that knows its data: the email field validates its shape and summons the @ keyboard on phones; the number field steps between 1 and 10 and refuses letters; the range renders as a slider bounded by the same kind of min/max; color opens a native color picker and always submits a #rrggbb value; file opens the OS file dialog restricted to images and allows several at once; and hidden submits its fixed pair without rendering anything. All of them are still just inputs — name and value semantics are unchanged.
lessons.example:
A phone user meets a plain text field asking for an email and has to fish for the @ symbol through three keyboard layers. The same field as type="email" opens the keyboard with @ and . ready — and quietly refuses 'ana@' as incomplete on submit.

The upgrade cost one word in the markup. That is the recurring deal in this lesson: precise types buy behaviour you would otherwise write, test and maintain yourself.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, finish the review form: make the email field a real email input, constrain the rating with number min/max/step, add a sweetness slider, scope the photo upload to images with accept, and carry the product id in a hidden input.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows a labelled form with an email field, a stepping number box for rating, a slider, a file chooser, and no visible trace of the hidden product id — with all five checks green.
commonMistakes: Trusting client-side validation as security. Every constraint — type, min, max, accept — can be bypassed by editing the page or crafting a request; the server must revalidate everything.
Using type="number" for phone numbers or ids. Leading zeros vanish and steppers make no sense; digit-like codes are tel or text, not numbers.
Adding a file input to a form without method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data" — the upload silently degrades to sending just the filename.
Treating hidden inputs as secret. They are invisible, not protected: anyone can read and alter them in DevTools, so never put trusted-as-is values there.
lessons.proTip: Pair a range with an <output> element to show its live value — <input type="range" id="s"> <output for="s">50</output> — and one line of JS keeps it updated. A slider whose current value is invisible is a guess, not a control.

coding.intro: You will upgrade a review form from generic text boxes to precise input types, constraining values in the markup and carrying hidden context.

sections.heading: Text-like with built-in meaning: email, url, tel, search
sections.body:
Four types look like text fields but declare their content. type="email" expects an email address: browsers check the basic shape (something@something) during native validation and, crucially, mobile keyboards switch to a layout with @ and dot prominent. Add the multiple attribute and the field accepts a comma-separated list of addresses.

type="url" expects an absolute URL and validates that shape (https://... passes; a bare word does not). type="tel" is for phone numbers — it brings up the dial-pad keyboard on phones but deliberately validates nothing, because worldwide phone formats are too varied; add pattern or server checks if you need strictness. type="search" behaves like text but signals search semantics: some browsers add a clear (×) button and style history differently.

The shared lesson: these types cost nothing over type="text" and buy keyboard, validation and semantics. When a field has a more precise type, use it — text is the fallback, not the default choice.
sections.code:
<input type="email" name="email">
<input type="url" name="website">
<input type="tel" name="phone">
<input type="search" name="q">

sections.heading: number: min, max and step
sections.body:
type="number" accepts numeric input only: letters are rejected as typed in most browsers, spinner arrows let users step the value, and three attributes define the legal space. min and max bound the range; a value outside them fails native validation on submit. step sets the stepping increment and the validity grid — step="1" (the default) allows integers, step="0.5" allows halves, and step="any" allows any number, which you need for free decimal input like prices or measurements.

The grid detail bites in practice: with min="1" and step="2", valid values are 1, 3, 5... — a typed 4 is invalid even though it is inside the range. Steps count from min (or from 0 if no min is set).

Just as important is when not to use number: any 'digits that are not a quantity'. Phone numbers, postal codes, credit cards and ids lose leading zeros, gain absurd spinners, and may trip locale formatting. If you would never compute an average of the field, it is not a number — use tel or text with a pattern.
sections.code:
<label for="rating">Rating (1–10)</label>
<input type="number" id="rating" name="rating"
       min="1" max="10" step="1">

<!-- decimals allowed: -->
<input type="number" name="price" min="0" step="any">

sections.heading: range: the slider — always show its value
sections.body:
type="range" renders as a drag slider for choosing a number where the feel is approximate: volume, brightness, sweetness. It shares number's min, max and step attributes (defaults 0, 100, 1), and value positions the initial thumb — omit it and the thumb starts at the midpoint.

The honest limitation: a slider hides its number. The user sees a position, not a value, and the exact figure submitted is invisible. The standard cure is pairing the slider with an output element — a semantic element meant exactly for displaying a calculation or control result — plus a small script keeping it current. If the precise number matters to the user (a price limit, a quantity), prefer type="number" outright; ranges are for relative settings.

Submission is unchanged from any input: name=value with the thumb's current number. One accessibility note: keyboard users adjust the slider with arrow keys, which is why respecting a sensible step matters.
sections.code:
<label for="sweetness">Sweetness</label>
<input type="range" id="sweetness" name="sweetness"
       min="0" max="100" step="10" value="50">
<output for="sweetness">50</output>

sections.heading: color: a native picker in one attribute
sections.body:
type="color" renders a small swatch that opens the operating system's colour picker on click. No library, no palette widget — the whole picker is one attribute.

Its contract is strict and simple: the value is always a seven-character lowercase hex string in the form #rrggbb. That is what value must contain to preselect a colour (invalid initial values fall back to #000000, black), and exactly what submits. No alpha channel, no named colours, no shorthand #369 — normalise before and after.

Use cases are narrower than the other types — theme accent choices, label colours, drawing tools — but where it fits, it replaces significant custom UI. As with all of this lesson's controls, pair it with a real label; the bare swatch says nothing about what the colour is for.
sections.code:
<label for="accent">Accent colour</label>
<input type="color" id="accent" name="accent" value="#336699">
<!-- submits: accent=%23336699 (the # encoded) -->

sections.heading: file: uploads with accept and multiple
sections.body:
type="file" renders a button that opens the OS file dialog; the chosen filename appears beside it. Two attributes shape the dialog. accept filters which files the picker offers, taking a comma-separated list of MIME types, wildcards or extensions: accept="image/*" for any image, accept=".pdf,.docx" for specific formats, accept="image/png,image/jpeg" for exact types. multiple allows selecting several files at once.

Two hard requirements from the forms-basics lesson come due here: the form must use method="post" and enctype="multipart/form-data", the only encoding that can carry file bytes. Without it, submission does not fail loudly — the server just receives the filename as text, an error you find days later.

Two trust warnings. accept filters the dialog for convenience; users can often override it, and a crafted request can send anything — the server must verify actual file type and size. And for privacy, a file input's value cannot be preset by markup or script; only the user can pick files, which is why you cannot 're-fill' a file field after a failed submit.
sections.code:
<form action="/review" method="post"
      enctype="multipart/form-data">
  <label for="photo">Photos of your dish</label>
  <input type="file" id="photo" name="photo"
         accept="image/*" multiple>
</form>

sections.heading: hidden: data the user never edits
sections.body:
type="hidden" renders nothing at all — no box, no label needed — yet submits its name=value pair like any field. It exists to carry context the submission needs but the user should not edit: which product this review belongs to, which step of a wizard is being submitted, an anti-forgery (CSRF) token issued by the server, a tracking source code.

The value is typically written into the markup by the server when generating the page, then travels back on submit — a round trip that keeps stateless HTTP conversations coherent without cookies or JavaScript.

The security boundary must be exact in your head: hidden means not rendered, nothing more. Any user can open DevTools, read the value and change it before submitting. So hidden fields may carry identifiers and tokens the server verifies, but never authority the server trusts blindly — a hidden price=0.01 that the checkout believes is the textbook exploit. Validate hidden values exactly as sceptically as visible ones.
sections.code:
<input type="hidden" name="product-id" value="prod-8841">
<!-- invisible in the page, present in the submission -->

lessons.title: Pick dates and times with the five date-time input types
lessons.summary: Use date, time, datetime-local, month and week inputs, master their exact value formats, constrain them with min/max/step, and degrade gracefully where support is missing.
lessons.goal: Build an appointment booking form with native date and time pickers, bounded ranges, and value formats you can read and write by hand.
lessons.whyItMatters: Date entry is one of the most error-prone parts of any form — day/month order differs by country, typos create impossible dates, and custom picker widgets are heavy and often inaccessible. The native date-time inputs solve all of this: localised pickers for free, impossible dates unpickable, and one unambiguous wire format (ISO 8601) reaching your server regardless of the user's locale. Knowing the formats and the support caveats is what makes them safe to rely on.
steps: Read date and its YYYY-MM-DD value format.
Read time, then datetime-local and its T-joined format.
Skim month and week — rarer, but they complete the family.
Study min, max and step as they apply to dates and times.
Read the support and graceful-degradation section before trusting any of this in production.
In the editor, complete tasks 1–5 and test the pickers in the preview.
lessons.prompt:
<input type="date" name="day"
       min="2026-08-10" max="2026-12-31">

<input type="time" name="start" min="09:00" max="17:00" step="900">

<input type="datetime-local" name="delivery"
       value="2026-08-15T14:30">

<input type="month" name="billing" value="2026-08">
lessons.explanation: Each control opens a native picker and speaks one fixed wire format: the date is bounded to a booking window and will submit like day=2026-08-20; the time field limits picks to office hours in 15-minute steps (step is in seconds, so 900); datetime-local combines both with a literal T between them and no timezone; month drops the day entirely. Whatever format the user sees on screen — 20/08/2026 in Athens, 8/20/2026 in Chicago — the submitted value is always the ISO form on the left.
lessons.example:
A booking form with a plain text date field receives '3/4/2026' — March in one country, April in another — plus '31/02/2026' from typos and 'next Tuesday' from optimists. Every record needs parsing, guessing and apologising.

The same field as type="date" shows each user a calendar in their own format, makes February 31st unpickable, and delivers 2026-04-03 to the server every single time. The ambiguity does not need handling because it can no longer occur.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, build the booking form's scheduling fields: a date picker bounded to the clinic's booking window, a time picker for office hours, a datetime-local field for the follow-up call, and a month picker for the payment plan.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview shows four labelled picker fields; opening the date field displays a calendar that refuses dates outside the window, and all five checks pass.
commonMistakes: Writing localised values into value, min or max — value="20/08/2026" is simply ignored. The wire format is always ISO: YYYY-MM-DD, HH:MM, YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM.
Assuming datetime-local carries a timezone. It is deliberately 'local, unspecified': for events pinned to a global instant, the server must combine it with a separately captured zone.
Forgetting that step on time inputs counts seconds. step="15" means 15 seconds, not minutes — a quarter-hour grid is step="900".
Trusting the picker as validation. Unsupported browsers fall back to a bare text field, and crafted requests can send anything — the server revalidates format and range, always.
lessons.proTip: The ISO formats sort correctly as plain strings — 2026-08-09 < 2026-08-10 alphabetically. That is not a coincidence; it is why year comes first, and it means you can sort and compare submitted dates without parsing them.

coding.intro: You will equip a clinic booking form with the native date-time inputs, bounding each one so impossible appointments cannot be picked.

sections.heading: date: a calendar in one attribute
sections.body:
input type="date" gives the user a full calendar picker: browsers render a field that opens a month grid, with year and month navigation, localised day names, and impossible dates simply not offered. The user experience — clicking a day on a calendar — took whole JavaScript libraries to build before this type existed.

Its value format is the heart of the matter: always YYYY-MM-DD, zero-padded, regardless of what the user sees. A German user sees and types 20.08.2026, an American sees 08/20/2026 — both fields submit day=2026-08-20. Display is localised; the wire format is universal. The same ISO form is what you must write when presetting value, and what min and max expect.

The field submits its name with the ISO string, or an empty value when nothing was picked — combine with the required attribute if a date is mandatory. There is no way to express 'partial' dates here; for a month without a day, a dedicated type exists later in this lesson.
sections.code:
<label for="day">Appointment date</label>
<input type="date" id="day" name="day" value="2026-08-20">
<!-- submits: day=2026-08-20, whatever the local display -->

sections.heading: time: hours and minutes, no day
sections.body:
input type="time" collects a time of day with no date attached, rendering a spinner or dropdown-style picker depending on the browser and platform. Twelve- versus twenty-four-hour display follows the user's system settings; as with dates, the presentation is localised while the value is fixed.

That value format is HH:MM in 24-hour form — 09:00, 14:30, 23:05 — zero-padded on both sides. If seconds are relevant (they rarely are), the format extends to HH:MM:SS, and browsers show a seconds slot only when the step attribute demands that precision.

A time value alone means 'this time of day, wherever you are': a daily alarm, opening hours, a recurring meeting slot. It carries no timezone and no date, which is exactly right for those cases — and exactly wrong for one-off global events, which is what the next type addresses.
sections.code:
<label for="start">Preferred time</label>
<input type="time" id="start" name="start" value="09:30">
<!-- submits: start=09:30 (24-hour wire format) -->

sections.heading: datetime-local: both at once, no timezone
sections.body:
input type="datetime-local" combines the two pickers into one control collecting a date and a time together. Its value format joins the two previous formats with a literal capital T: 2026-08-15T14:30. Write it exactly so in value, min and max; the submitted value has the same shape.

The name's suffix is a specification, not decoration: the value is local and timezone-less. '15 August, 14:30' — but 14:30 where? The control does not say, and that is by design. For an in-person appointment at a clinic, the location is implied and the type is perfect. For a webinar joined from three continents, a naked local datetime is a bug factory: the server must also know the relevant timezone, captured separately (a select of zones, or JavaScript reading the browser's), and convert to UTC for storage.

A historical note you will meet in old code: an input type="datetime" (with timezone) once existed in the spec and was abandoned — browsers treat it as text. datetime-local is the one that survived.
sections.code:
<label for="followup">Follow-up call</label>
<input type="datetime-local" id="followup" name="followup"
       value="2026-08-15T14:30">
<!-- submits: followup=2026-08-15T14:30 -->

sections.heading: month and week: the coarse pickers
sections.body:
Two coarser-grained types complete the family. input type="month" collects a month within a year — value format YYYY-MM, like 2026-08 — with a picker that skips days entirely. It fits billing periods, card expiry dates and report months: anywhere a day number would be noise.

input type="week" collects an ISO week within a year, value format YYYY-Www — 2026-W33 is the 33rd week of 2026. ISO weeks start on Monday, and week 1 is the week containing the year's first Thursday, so the first days of January can belong to the previous year's last week; planning and logistics domains use this numbering, and the input speaks it natively.

Honest guidance: these two have the weakest browser support of the family — several browsers render them as plain text fields — so they are exactly where the degradation strategy of the last section matters most. If your audience skews to unsupported browsers, two selects (month + year) remain a reasonable substitute for month.
sections.code:
<label for="billing">First billing month</label>
<input type="month" id="billing" name="billing" value="2026-09">

<label for="delivery-week">Delivery week</label>
<input type="week" id="delivery-week" name="delivery-week" value="2026-W38">

sections.heading: min, max and step on dates and times
sections.body:
The constraint attributes you know from number apply across the whole family, expressed in each type's own value format. A booking window is two attributes: min="2026-08-10" max="2026-12-31" on a date input makes earlier and later days unpickable in the calendar and invalid on submit. Office hours on a time input: min="09:00" max="17:00".

step is where units demand attention. On time and datetime-local inputs, step counts seconds: a 15-minute appointment grid is step="900", and any step below 60 makes browsers reveal a seconds field. On date inputs, step counts days (step="7" allows only every seventh day from min — a crude weekly grid); on month inputs it counts months, and on week inputs, weeks.

Two reminders complete the picture. Constraints participate in native validation — the form refuses to submit with an out-of-range value and shows a browser message — and they are advisory at the network level, so range-checking on the server remains mandatory. And min/max only bound static windows; 'no earlier than today' needs the server or a script to write today's date into min when generating the page.
sections.code:
<!-- Booking window, office hours, quarter-hour grid -->
<input type="date" name="day"
       min="2026-08-10" max="2026-12-31">
<input type="time" name="start"
       min="09:00" max="17:00" step="900">

sections.heading: Browser support and graceful degradation
sections.body:
Support across the family is uneven: date, time and datetime-local enjoy solid support in current browsers, while month and week are still missing in several — and any unknown type falls back to a plain text input. That fallback is the family's built-in safety net, and designing for it is what makes these types production-safe.

The fallback field still submits under its name, so the data flow survives; what disappears is the picker, the format enforcement and the constraints. Three habits make the degraded experience acceptable. State the expected format in the label or a hint ('YYYY-MM-DD') so text-mode users can comply. Never let the placeholder be the only format documentation. And validate format and range on the server, which you were doing anyway — the fallback simply makes that non-negotiable.

You can detect support in JavaScript when you need to know: create an input, set its type, and read the property back — an unsupported type reads as 'text' — then mount a fallback widget only where necessary. But start from the native control and add machinery only when evidence demands it: the native pickers are localised, accessible and maintained by the browser, which is a bar most custom widgets never reach.
